title: Nighttime temperature to daytime function: Sleep improvements with the Pod
summary: Poor sleep is rarely caused by just one thing, yet most sleep solutions aim to ameliorate only one problem. For example, a cooling mattress pad addresses overnight heat.
body_markdown:
Poor sleep is rarely caused by just one thing, yet most sleep solutions aim to ameliorate only one problem. For example, a cooling mattress pad addresses overnight heat. A meditation app addresses pre-sleep anxiety. A sleep restriction protocol addresses insomnia. And even when a solution targets the right problem, most still require ongoing effort to experience benefits over time. You may have to continuously track patterns, build and maintain new routines, or actively reshape how you think about sleep, night after night.


A longitudinal study of 254 Eight Sleep members tracked subjective sleep metrics across five time points, starting before Pod use and continuing through one week, two weeks, one month, and six months of sleeping on the Pod. The findings reveal a four-stage pathway to[sustained sleep improvements](https://www.eightsleep.com/blog/sleep-improvements-that-actually-last-how-the-pod-outperforms-sleep-trackers) and daytime functioning: the thermal sleep environment improves, negative beliefs about sleep decrease, behaviors supporting sleep improve, and sleep outcomes improve.


## **Key takeaways:**


After beginning to sleep on the Pod:


1. Thermal comfort improved within one week and held through six months; bed-too-hot at bedtime complaints dropped by 87% on average after one month.


2. Dysfunctional beliefs about sleep decreased within the first two weeks; sleep anxiety decreased by 38% on average.


3. Sleep hygiene behaviors improved by 15% on average one month and did not reverse, even six months later.


4. Insomnia symptoms decreased by 34-46% on average, subjective sleep quality improved by 42% on average, and daytime functioning improved by 39% on average after one month, all showing clinically meaningful improvement.


## **How the Pod improves your sleep in a four-stage pathway**


### **Stage 1: The thermal sleep environment improves with the Pod**


The thermal sleep environment directly affects sleep quality.


Temperature, noise, light, and bedding comfort all influence how easily the body transitions into and maintains sleep (


[source](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0360132318300325) ).


Of these factors, temperature stands out for a specific reason: it’s not just an input from the environment; it’s built into the body systems that trigger sleep onset (


[source](https://doi.org/10.3389/fnins.2019.00336) ).


Core body temperature must drop 2-3°F to initiate sleep onset and remain low throughout the first half of the night to maintain sleep (


[source](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1087079207000950?via%3Dihub) ,


[source](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18192289/) ).


When the bed surface is too hot, this process can be interrupted, and sleep suffers before it even starts (


[source](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1087079208000117?via%3Dihub) ).


Complaints of the bed being too hot at bedtime decreased after one week of sleeping on the Pod and stayed low even 6 months later (Figure).


**Figure.** Reported complaints of the bed feeling too hot at bedtime after beginning to sleep on the Pod. All reported percent changes are average values displayed on the y-axis (%). Time after beginning to sleep on the Pod is represented on the x-axis (weeks & months)


By resolving the most immediate barrier to sleep onset and early-night maintenance, bed-temperature regulation creates the conditions for the remaining three stages to follow.


### **Stage 2: Pod use decreases negative beliefs about sleep**


According to the Dysfunctional Beliefs and Attitude Scale, dysfunctional sleep beliefs are unhelpful thoughts and attitudes about sleep, such as catastrophizing a bad night, feeling like you need exactly eight hours to function, or believing a sleeping pill is the only solution (


[source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2082102/) ).


These beliefs make sleep worse by increasing anxiety around bedtime (


[source](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12186352/) ).


The current gold-standard approach for correcting these beliefs is Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I), a structured, multi-week program that directly targets dysfunctional sleep beliefs among other insomnia drivers (


[source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5797481/) ).


After only one week of sleeping on the Pod, overall dysfunctional sleep beliefs decreased by 9%, on average.


- Specific belief changes within the first two weeks included:


- “I need to catch up on sleep after a bad night”: decreased by 38% on average


- “A sleeping pill is better than a bad night’s sleep”: decreased by 34% on average


- “I need exactly eight hours to function”: decreased by 12% on average


These changes are notable because CBT-I requires ongoing effort, making its behavioral demands hard to sustain (


[source](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-87018-3) ). Unfortunately, without any intervention, dysfunctional sleep beliefs barely shift.


In a previous study, a group with no intervention saw only about a 3% change over six weeks (


[source](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-87018-3) ).


Here, beliefs shifted by 9% within the first two weeks, passively, as a downstream effect of the thermal sleep environment change and mindset improvements.


### **Stage 3: Sleep hygiene improved after beginning to sleep on the Pod**


Sleep hygiene refers to the habits and behaviors that support consistent, restful sleep, such as keeping a regular sleep schedule, avoiding work or screens in bed, and limiting worry at bedtime (


[source](https://www.eightsleep.com/blog/tips-on-how-to-have-the-best-sleep-hygiene/) ).


Sleep hygiene behaviors improved alongside belief changes. It could be that as beliefs around sleep improved, individuals were motivated to change their behaviors to better align with the new, more helpful beliefs. More research is needed to test this assumption.


- After one month of sleeping on the Pod, overall sleep hygiene behavior scores improved by 15% on average. Specific changes included a 15% average reduction in worrying or planning while in bed, and an 11% average reduction in doing work before bed.


- After six months of sleeping on the Pod, sleep hygiene behavior scores remained improved by 13% on average.


Together, these three stages reveal a consistent pattern: each change occurred passively, without the need for CBT-I, outside of coaching, or deliberate behavior changes. These stages laid the foundation for the meaningful outcomes that followed.


### **Stage 4: Insomnia symptoms decreased with the Pod, while subjective sleep quality improved**


Subjective sleep outcomes are measured using validated survey instruments, the same tools clinicians use to assess and monitor sleep conditions. Improvements in insomnia symptoms, subjective sleep quality, and daytime functioning all reached clinically meaningful levels one month after beginning to sleep on the Pod and were sustained through six months.


### Insomnia symptoms


- Overall insomnia symptoms decreased by 34-46% on average up to six months after beginning to sleep on the Pod, comparable to CBT-I, which reduces insomnia symptoms by 40-50% on average in meta-analyses (


[source](https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/M14-2841?url_ver=Z39.88-2003&rfr_id=ori:rid:crossref.org&rfr_dat=cr_pub%20%200pubmed) ,


[source](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1087079217300345?via%3Dihub) ).


- Terminal insomnia, waking too early and being unable to return to sleep, decreased by 45% on average after one week of sleeping on the Pod and by 46% on average after six months.


- Maintenance insomnia, difficulty staying asleep, decreased by 37% on average after two weeks of sleeping on the Pod and by 45% on average after one month.


### Subjective sleep quality


- Subjective sleep quality improved by 42% on average after one month of sleeping on the Pod and by 28% on average after six months.


- Both improvements exceed the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) threshold for clinically meaningful change, which is a reduction of three or more points for each component of the survey (there are 7 components;


[source](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0165178189900474?via%3Dihub) ).


This indicates that members experienced improvements large enough to be impactful in daily life.


### Daytime functioning


- Daytime functioning improved by 39% on average after one month of sleeping on the Pod and by 34% on average after six months.


- 59% of participants reported reduced daytime sleepiness after one month of sleeping on the Pod.


## **What do all of these changes mean for your sleep?**


Each stage builds on the previous one, from temperature regulation through clinically meaningful improvements in sleep quality and daytime functioning. Improvements are reported within one week of beginning to sleep on the Pod and hold through six months.


For individuals looking to improve their sleep, a single sleep environment change can produce improvements that rival therapy, medication, or structured behavioral intervention.


Also, unlike medications for insomnia, which are generally intended only for short-term use (


[source](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/treatments/cognitive-behavioral-therapy-insomnia) ), changing the sleep environment can be a long-term solution.


We found that sleep improvements held for six months (the longest timepoint we measured) without any ongoing intervention. These findings suggest that addressing the thermal sleep environment directly may offer a more comprehensive path to optimal sleep and daytime functioning than targeting any one domain.

## **Appendix: Study details**


*All findings presented above are statistically significant at the Bonferroni-corrected alpha level of 0.025, using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.*


*Two hundred and fifty-four Eight Sleep members completed seven validated clinical surveys before Pod use and at one week, two weeks, one month, and six months. The surveys administered were the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), American Academy of Sleep Medicine survey (AASM), Sleep Hygiene Index (SHI), Dysfunctional Beliefs and Attitudes about Sleep scale (DBAS), and Snore Outcomes Survey (SOS). Sample sizes at each timepoint ranged from n=83 at one week to n=27-33 at six months. Analysis used non-parametric statistical tests with Bonferroni correction throughout.*
